question: English laws never expire on their own. Which of these are still in force, and which were finally repealed?
answer: A law stays until Parliament spends time removing it, so what survives is what nobody bothered to fight. Royal fish and the 1313 armour ban harm no one and stand. Laws that could still bite drew campaigns: blasphemy went only in 2008, sedition in 2009, and a medium was jailed as a witch in 1944.
move: Old rules survive when keeping them costs nobody anything.

items.note: Whales and sturgeon caught off the coast belong to the Crown.
items.verdict: From a statute of about 1324, never repealed. Stranded whales still go to the Crown.

items.note: Insulting the Christian faith is a crime.
items.verdict: Abolished in England and Wales only in 2008.

items.note: Coming to Parliament in armour is forbidden.
items.verdict: A statute of 1313, still in force.

items.note: Claiming to conjure spirits is a crime.
items.verdict: Repealed in 1951. A medium was jailed under it in 1944.

items.note: Being drunk in charge of cattle on a road.
items.verdict: An offence under the Licensing Act 1872, still in force.

items.note: Stirring up hatred of the Crown or government in print.
items.verdict: A crime until 2009, when Parliament abolished it.

reference: https://www.legislation.gov.uk (Prerogativa Regis; Statute Forbidding Bearing of Armour 1313; Licensing Act 1872 s.12; Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008 s.79; Coroners and Justice Act 2009 s.73; Fraudulent Mediums Act 1951)
